title: Phonics FAQ
author: Christopher Such
summary: Christopher Such uses a question-and-answer format, drawn from years of recurring social-media debates, to lay out a comprehensive defense of systematic synthetic phonics as the correct starting point for reading instruction — while carefully bounding its scope. He explains the alphabetic code precisely, defines systematic synthetic phonics against alternative approaches like whole-word memorization and cueing strategies, and argues that both alternatives seduce with early apparent success before stranding struggling readers once texts grow more complex. Crucially, Such rejects the common criticism that phonics has crowded out other aspects of literacy instruction, stating flatly that in his direct experience with many schools he has never found one that stopped developing spoken language or sharing books because of a phonics mandate. The piece's most pointed argument addresses why key-stage-2 reading outcomes remain disappointing despite improved phonics screening scores: Such argues the phonics check only ever measured initial decoding, and that the real failure lies in how key-stage-2 reading is taught, with too much time spent on fragmented comprehension-question drilling and too little on actual sustained reading practice. He closes by defending pseudo-word testing on the phonics screening check as a deliberate design choice to verify genuine decoding ability rather than memorized sight recognition.
points: Such's core structural claim — that whole-word memorization and cueing strategies both 'seductively offer initial success before leaving pupils stranded as texts grow more challenging' — reframes debates about early reading gains as potentially misleading if not tracked into later, harder texts.

His direct empirical claim, based on extensive school experience, that he has never found a school that dropped spoken-language development or book-sharing because of a phonics mandate directly rebuts a commonly repeated criticism of systematic phonics without relying on abstract argument.

By locating the cause of disappointing key-stage-2 reading outcomes in how reading is taught after initial decoding — 'precious little actual reading' amid endless fragmented comprehension questions — rather than in phonics itself, Such redirects blame away from the policy critics most often target.
quotes: The English writing system is alphabetic. This means that letters of the alphabet are used to represent phonemes.

Synthetic phonics involves explicitly teaching pupils about the way that phonemes are represented in words from the very beginning of instruction so that pupils can start decoding and spelling words straight away.

Trying to learn all words as whole units is a dead-end strategy for pupils. This strategy is all the more destructive because it seductively offers initial success before leaving pupils stranded as the texts they read become more challenging.

I am yet to find a single school that stopped developing pupils' spoken language capabilities or sharing wonderful books because they were required to follow a systematic plan in teaching pupils to decode.
By asking pupils to decode pseudo-words, we can find out whether pupils are able to apply what they have learned from phonics to unfamiliar words.

Bluntly, in far too many schools the teaching of reading in key stage 2 involves precious little actual reading. Instead pupils are often introduced to small chunks of text, about which they answer different question types for hours on end.
